query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: If, under elevated-temperature service conditions, Mg atoms in a metastable lightweight high-entropy alloy rapidly partition out of the supersaturated solid solution to form Mg-rich intermetallics near grain boundaries, these precipitates will locally deplete passivating elements from the matrix, disrupt protective oxide scale integrity, and thereby reduce the alloy’s corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, Mg-containing lightweight HEA produced via non-equilibrium processing, with minimal intermetallics and partial short-range ordering present in the as-cast or as-quenched condition.
generation.intervention: Utilize real-time in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction or high-resolution TEM heating trials to track the nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases during controlled thermal exposure, then evaluate changes in corrosion and oxidation resistance at intermediate and final stages of transformation.
generation.conditions: Samples will be held at temperatures up to ~600 °C in air for times ranging from minutes to several hours, followed by exposures to a standard corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) to gauge changes in passivation and corrosion rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Emergent Mg-rich intermetallic phases forming at grain boundaries and within the matrix, leading to elemental partitioning away from the protective solid solution.
generation.mechanism: Local clustering of Mg under thermal activation drives intermetallic precipitation, causing depletion of key protective elements from the matrix and disrupting uniform oxide films, thereby increasing susceptibility to both high-temperature oxidation and corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial state, in situ observation will reveal new phase reflections (or contrast in TEM) attributable to intermetallic compounds. Corrosion and oxidation tests will show reduced passivation efficacy (evidenced by increased mass loss, higher corrosion current, or more spallation) in samples after sufficient thermal soak.
generation.baseline: The as-processed, single-phase metastable solid solution with no observable intermetallics and stable passivation behavior.
generation.boundary: Below ~400–500 °C or with insufficient dwell time, Mg partitioning and intermetallic precipitation should be minimal, preserving corrosion/oxidation resistance. Above these temperatures or at longer times, precipitation accelerates, leading to a measurable performance decline.
generation.uncertainty: The kinetics and exact precipitation morphologies for Mg-rich compounds are currently unverified due to lack of direct Mg-specific studies in the available literature references.

falsification_experiment.design: Continuously monitor phase evolution at elevated temperatures using in situ synchrotron-based diffraction or advanced in situ TEM. Quench and remove specimens at specified intervals for detailed microstructural and surface-chemistry analysis via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and scanning/transmission electron microscopy. Subsequently, perform electrochemical corrosion tests and high-temperature oxidation measurements on these quenched samples.
measurements: Appearance and growth rate of any new diffraction peaks indicating Mg-rich intermetallics
Quantitative compositional analysis near precipitates (EDS or APT)
Surface oxide morphology, thickness, and adhesion (SEM/TEM)
Potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy for corrosion resistance
Mass gain/loss and oxide spallation during isothermal oxidation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If elevated-temperature exposure does not induce Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation or if no significant change in corrosion or oxidation resistance is observed despite the thermal treatment, then the hypothesis that Mg partitioning triggers intermetallic formation leading to property degradation must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are among the promising candidates for the design of structural materials in advanced nuclear energy systems. The effects of Cr, V, Ta, and Ti elements and ball milling on the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of model RHEAs were investigated. The results show that W-rich BCC1 and Ta-rich BCC2 solid solution phases were generated after a long milling duration. After high-temperature sintering, the (Cr, Ta)-rich phase associated with the Laves phase was observed in the Cr-containing model RHEAs. In addition, a high level of Ti, Ta, and V contents promoted the in situ formation of oxide particles in the alloys. Complex TiTa2O7 and Ta2VO6 oxide phases were identified by TEM, which suggests a solid-state reaction of Ti-O, Ta-O, and V-O subjected to high-energy ball milling. The oxide particles are uniformly dispersed in the BCC matrix, which can result in dispersion strengthening and the enhancement of mechanical properties.

Collectively, these findings suggest that, similar to conventional alloys, HEAs undergo selective oxidation, with aluminum and chromium playing crucial roles in determining the oxidation behavior [,]. Previous studies have demonstrated that inert anodes used in aluminum electrolysis, made from medium-entropy alloys (Fe-Ni-Cu), exhibit excellent high-temperature stability and corrosion resistance. These alloys form a protective NiFe2O4 layer at elevated temperatures, significantly improving their corrosion resistance [,]. Building on this, this research aims to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behavior of FeNiCuAlCr, FeNiCuAlCo, and FeNiCuAlMn high-entropy alloys. The use of Cr, Co, and Mn in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) aims to enhance the various properties of the alloy. Cr primarily improves the alloy’s corrosion resistance and oxidation resistance by forming a stable protective oxide layer. Co enhances the high-temperature stability of the alloy and increases its strength, making it suitable for high-stress and high-temperature environments. Since the working pressures and temperatures must be very high to obtain the best turbine efficiency, materials with a high chemical, thermal, and mechanical stability are needed, to allow them to work under these extreme conditions. Due to their good stability and mechanical properties, high entropy alloys have been proposed for application in the construction of those turbine components that are most exposed to the action of the gases being burned in the turbine. Through observations and analysis with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), mapping was performed of each sample to verify the spatial distribution of the alloy components. Figure 5 shows a typical mapping of those performed on the different alloys. The elemental mapping indicated that the samples with sintered CrCuFeNiTiAlx alloys possessed a multi-phase microstructure, as can be seen in the figure by means of the labels placed on the different phases of the microstructure. In the mapping, spatial regions with a good distribution of alloying elements indicated the formation of the high entropy alloys sought here. From these results, it can be inferred that the microstructure of this alloy was composed of a high Cu, Fe, and Ni solid solution (light region); a dark region composed of Ti and Cr; and dispersed chromium and copper oxide phases.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC7579168, 2020) on Al–Mg-based lightweight complex concentrated alloys examined non-equilibrium solidification pathways and identified intermetallic phases forming under certain heat-treatment conditions, highlighting the challenge of stabilizing solid solutions. Subsequent research (PMC11330973, 2024) showed that, under high pressure and temperature, Al–Mg-dominant CCAs could achieve single-phase microstructures with improved mechanical performance and reduced intermetallic formation. More recently (PMC12508472, 2025), attention turned to the role of non-equilibrium chemical short-range order, underscoring how kinetic pathways and processing histories can drive transformations and determine eventual microstructure. Despite these advances, the detailed mechanisms governing the transient metastable state and its effect on corrosion and oxidation resistance remain unclear.
decision.unsolved: It is not yet established precisely how and when intermetallic compounds form during thermal or service conditions in Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy (or complex concentrated) alloys, or how the evolving short-range order and partitioning of Mg among phases impact corrosion and high-temperature oxidation response. The interplay between transformation kinetics, local chemical environments, and the onset of damaging phase formation has not been pinpointed, leaving gaps in our ability to predict and control the final microstructure and performance.
decision.lever: Employ real-time in-situ synchrotron/advanced TEM heating trials to track intermetallic precipitation and Mg partitioning in a controlled temperature-time exposure relevant to elevated service conditions (up to ~600 °C). Corrosion and oxidation tests can then be performed on samples removed at intermediate stages to correlate evolving microstructure with changes in environmental resistance.
decision.why: Because the literature highlights the critical role of non-equilibrium states and short-range order in microstructural evolution, directly observing the transformation pathways under representative service environments is the most logical next step. In-situ advanced characterization will allow researchers to validate or refute the proposed hypothesis about how Mg solute clustering and intermetallic precipitation modify local chemistry, thereby influencing oxide film adherence and corrosion performance in this complex, metastable alloy system.
